newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bank sector rocked by mega-merger.
newsitem.headline: German bank sector rocked by mega-merger.

text.p: The reformation of Germany's banking industry began Monday with two Bavarian banks unveiling a bold plan to merge in a deal that will create a German banking giant second only to the mighty Deutsche Bank AG.

Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechselbank AG -- both Bavarian specialists in mortgage lending and ranked fourth and fifth respectively among publicly listed commercial banks -- said they would merge as equal partners to form Bayerische Hypo- und Vereinsbank AG.

The new bank will be a powerful force in German banking, a sector seen as ripe for consolidation. It will have combined assets of 743 billion marks ($416 billion), toppling Dresdner Bank AG, the current No. 2, and not far off Deutsche, which in 1996 had total assets of 886 billion marks ($495 million).

It will concentrate on retail banking, property finance and asset management and will be Europe's leading mortgage bank, the banks said, adding that it will not shy away from foreign acquisitions to strengthen its investment banking business.
"I think it is not an exaggeration to say that this is the realisation of a vision in Europe's banking market," Hypo-Bank Chairman Eberhard Martini told a news conference.

"Hypo-Bank and Vereinsbank alone are too small to realise the economies of scale which are necessary on the enlarged market. By merging, they have reached a volume which will enable them to remain competitive and to act autonomously in the future European market."

The stock market's focus is now likely to shift to other potential merger candidates, heightening what had already been intense interest in bank shares. "The Gordian knot has been cut," one analyst said, predicting further mergers.
Analysts gave the merger a mixed reception, calling it a first major step toward consolidation in a market seen as hopelessly overbanked. But they doubted whether the new bank would shed enough jobs.

"The decision is right and positive for Munich as a financial centre," German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said. But he added that politicians would have to put pressure on the two banks to minimise job cuts.
Vereinsbank chairman Albrecht Schmidt and Hypo-Bank's Martini, both of whom have said they are available to head the new bank, refused to specify how many jobs of a combined 40,000 would be shed.

"We're not embarking on a cost defensive but on a quality offensive," Schmidt said. "We need every hard-working and qualified man and woman on board our larger ship in order to make progress on this stormy world market."
The banks together had staff turnover of 2,000 employees per year, Martini said. That meant any job cuts could be carried out in a "very gentle and socially acceptable way."

Investors gave the plans a firm thumbs-up, sending the two banks' stocks to all-time highs. Vereinsbank stock, which has nearly doubled on merger talk in the past year, rose 3.4 percent to 85.70 while Hypo-Bank jumped 14 percent to 66.70 marks, having earlier traded as high as 74 marks.

Under the deal, Vereinsbank will swap four-fifths of its 10 percent stake in insurer Allianz AG for shares in Hypo-Bank, offering one Allianz share for six Hypo-Bank shares. That values Hypo-Bank shares at 75 marks, giving a 28 percent premium on the closing price of 58.50 marks on July 18.
Vereinsbank will obtain up to 45 percent of Hypo-Bank. After the swap Vereinsbank will raise capital by a nominal 150 million marks ($83.8 million) to boost the new bank's equity base.

The merger is expected to cost around 1.3 billion marks ($726 million) in restructuring costs, but the banks said it would also cut expenses by as much as 1 billion marks ($559 million) per year in five years and spark a "marked increase" in earnings.

Analysts had mixed views of the plan. Commerzbank immediately raised its recommendation on the top five listed German banking stocks to a "buy," while Salomon reduced its recommendation on Vereinsbank to "hold" from "buy."
Salomon analyst Matthew Czepliewicz said he was concerned that the new bank would not be able to achieve its earnings goals because of political pressure not to cut too many jobs.
The deal will be presented to shareholders for approval by spring 1998. The German cartel office must also approve, but analysts said this was unlikely to be problematic.
